title: Reporting people's words and thoughts
subtitle: She explained that she couldn't take the job.
summary: Report words and thoughts in your own words or as a quotation, put the negative in the right clause, and report both wh- and yes/no questions.

lesson.heading: Reporting clause + reported clause
lesson.text: When we report what people think or say, we usually give the information in our own words. The sentence has a **reporting clause** and a **reported clause**.

examples.text: **She explained** (that) *she couldn't take the job until January*.
**He didn't tell me** *where to put the boxes*.

lesson.heading: Quoting the exact words
lesson.text: If the exact words matter, we report them as a quotation. The reporting clause can come before, within, or at the end of the quotation. In stories and novels the reporting verb often comes **before the subject** when the reporting clause follows the quotation - but never when the subject is a pronoun.

examples.text: 'I suppose you've heard the latest news,' **she said to me**.
'Of course,' **Carter replied**, 'you'll have to pay him to do the job.'
'And after that I moved to Italy,' **she continued**.

left.label: Negative in the reported clause
left.text: To report a negative sentence we normally make the reported clause negative.
examples: 'You're right, it isn't a good idea.' -> He agreed that it **wasn't** a good idea.
'I disagree. It's not a good idea at all.' -> He **didn't agree** that it was a good idea.
*The reporting clause goes negative here because he disagreed.*

right.label: Negative in the reporting clause
right.text: With believe, expect, feel, intend, plan, propose, suppose, think and want we usually make the reporting verb negative instead.
examples: 'I expect he won't come.' -> She **didn't expect** him to come.
not ~~She expected him not to come~~
He **didn't tell** me how he would get to London. *(= he said nothing about it)*

lesson.heading: Reporting wh-questions
lesson.text: To report a wh-question we use a reporting clause plus a clause with a wh-word. To report a yes/no question we use **if** or **whether**. Note that *if* can never be followed by a to-infinitive.

examples.text: She asked me **what the problem was**.
I asked him **where to go** next.
Liz wanted to know **if / whether** we had any photos of our holiday.

lesson.heading: Word order in the reported question
lesson.text: The wh-, if- or whether-clause has the word order of a **statement**, and we do not use a form of *do*. Exception: if we report a negative question, a negative form of *do* is possible.

examples.text: 'Have you seen Paul recently?' -> She wanted to know **if I had seen** Paul recently.
She asked me **where I found** it.
He asked (me) **why I didn't want** anything to eat.
examples.note: a reported negative question, so didn't is fine

lesson.heading: what / which / who + be
lesson.text: If the original question begins with **what**, **which** or **who** followed by *be* + complement, the complement can go before or after *be* in the report.

examples.text: 'Who was the winner?' -> I asked **who the winner was**.
'What are your long-term plans?' -> They asked **what my long-term plans were**.
examples.note: or ... what were my long-term plans.

lesson.text: Reported questions are statements, so they need statement word order and no auxiliary *do*: *where I found it*, not ~~where did I find it~~.

exercises.prompt: Match each quotation with the reporting verb that fits it.

pairs.left: 'Why don't we stop for a coffee?'

exercises.prompt: 'My novel is more exciting than a Dan Brown thriller,' she ___.
exercises.explanation: She is praising her own work, so the reporting verb is boasted.

exercises.prompt: Which report of 'And after that I moved to Italy' is correct?
options: 'And after that I moved to Italy,' she continued.
'And after that I moved to Italy,' continued she.
'And after that I moved to Italy,' continued.
exercises.explanation: The reporting verb can go before the subject after a quotation, but not when that subject is a pronoun.

exercises.prompt: Report the question 'Do you have any photos of your holiday?' - Liz asked it.
exercises.answer: Liz wanted to know if we had any photos of our holiday
alternatives: Liz wanted to know whether we had any photos of our holiday
exercises.explanation: A yes/no question is reported with if or whether plus statement word order.

exercises.statement: She asked me where did I find it.
exercises.explanation: She asked me where I found it. We do not use a form of do in the reported wh-clause.

exercises.prompt: 'Can you use a spreadsheet?' -> They wanted to know ___ use a spreadsheet.
exercises.explanation: A yes/no question becomes an if- or whether-clause, and can becomes could here.

exercises.prompt: 'Where did you learn Chinese?' -> They wondered ___ Chinese.
exercises.explanation: Statement word order, no did: where I (had) learnt Chinese.

exercises.prompt: To report a negative sentence, does the verb normally go negative in the reporting clause or in the reported clause?
categories: Negative reporting verb: didn't expect him to come
Negative reported clause: agreed that it wasn't a good idea

exercises.prompt: 'I won't give you the money back if you keep on at me.' -> He ___ the money if she kept on at him.
exercises.explanation: The threat itself is negative, so not goes before the to-infinitive: threatened not to repay.

exercises.prompt: 'I was surprised that Mum was angry.' -> He ___ his mother to be angry.
exercises.explanation: With expect we prefer a negative reporting verb: He didn't expect his mother to be angry.

exercises.prompt: 'I'm not going back to college.' -> She announced that she ___ back to college.
exercises.explanation: announce keeps its positive form; the negative belongs in the reported clause.

exercises.statement: He asked me why I didn't want anything to eat.
exercises.explanation: Correct. A reported negative question can keep a negative form of do.
